nameStory: Sweetberry honeysuckle gets its name from its uniquely sweet, edible berries - a rare treat among honeysuckles, most of which have bitter or even toxic fruits. The 'honeysuckle' part comes from the traditional practice of sucking the sweet nectar from the flowers, though this species is also known as 'honeyberry' for its delicious fruit. It's also called 'haskap,' a name borrowed from the Ainu people of northern Japan who have long treasured this arctic delicacy.
description: Sweetberry honeysuckle is a compact, non-climbing shrub that grows 3-5 feet tall and wide, making it quite different from the vigorous vining honeysuckles most people know. This cold-hardy northern species produces small, tubular yellowish-white flowers in early spring, followed by elongated blue berries that taste like a cross between blueberry and raspberry. The shrub has a neat, rounded growth habit with simple oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stems. It's one of the few honeysuckles native to New England's coldest regions.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Elongated blue berries about 1/2 to 3/4 inch long, often slightly flattened or oval rather than perfectly round, with a sweet-tart flavor and soft texture when ripe in early summer

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Dense, bushy shrub that stays compact at 3-5 feet tall, never climbing or vining like many other honeysuckles

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, paired tubular flowers that are pale yellow to creamy white, appearing very early in spring before many other plants have leafed out

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Simple oval leaves 1-3 inches long, arranged in opposite pairs, with a soft green color and slightly fuzzy texture, especially when young

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, while older bark develops a fibrous, shredding texture that peels in thin strips

habitat: In New England, sweetberry honeysuckle is extremely rare, found only in the coldest, most northern areas where it grows in moist, well-drained soils along woodland edges and in partially shaded clearings. It thrives in acidic to neutral soils and can tolerate both boggy conditions and rocky, well-drained sites. This arctic species reaches the very southern edge of its natural range in northern New England's high elevation areas.

seasonality.spring: Very early bloomer, producing small creamy flowers in April or early May, often before the leaves fully emerge. The flowers are among the first sources of nectar for early pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Distinctive blue berries ripen in June or July, earlier than most other wild berries in New England. Leaves are fully developed and soft green.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellow before dropping. The shrub's compact, rounded form becomes more apparent as surrounding vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the characteristic opposite branching pattern and fibrous, peeling bark on older stems. The dense, twiggy growth habit remains distinctive.

funFact: Sweetberry honeysuckle berries ripen so early in the season that they're often called 'June berries,' beating blueberries to the table by weeks and providing the year's first wild berry harvest when most other fruits are still just tiny green nubs.
confusionNotes: The blue berries might be confused with early blueberries, but sweetberry honeysuckle berries are more elongated and often grow in pairs, while blueberries are round and grow in clusters. Remember: 'Honeysuckle pairs, blueberries share (clusters).'
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the honeysuckle name fool you - this species is completely different from the aggressive, invasive honeysuckles that plague New England. While Japanese and other non-native honeysuckles are environmental problems, sweetberry honeysuckle is a rare native treasure that's more likely to be found in specialty gardens than in the wild.
compareHints: Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit. It's also much rarer and prefers colder conditions than the common invasive honeysuckles. The early-ripening blue berries are the dead giveaway - no other honeysuckle in New England has this combination of features.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
